claim: The STROBE is a closed-loop system for real-time optogenetic activation of feeding flies designed to evoke neural excitation coincident with food contact.
source: The STROBE is a closed-looped system for real-time optogenetic activation of feeding flies, designed to evoke neural excitation coincident with food contact.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the system developed.

claim: The STROBE's utility in probing the valence of fly sensory neurons was previously demonstrated by Jaeger et al., 2018.
source: We previously demonstrated the STROBE's utility in probing the valence of fly sensory neurons (Jaeger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: STROBE-driven behavior is modified by hunger.
source: Here we provide a thorough characterization of the STROBE system, demonstrate that STROBE-driven behavior is modified by hunger and the presence of taste ligands
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3.

claim: STROBE-driven behavior is modified by the presence of taste ligands.
source: Here we provide a thorough characterization of the STROBE system, demonstrate that STROBE-driven behavior is modified by hunger and the presence of taste ligands
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4.

claim: Mushroom body dopaminergic input neurons drive opposing feeding behaviors to their respective post-synaptic partners following activation.
source: find that mushroom body dopaminergic input neurons and their respective post-synaptic partners drive opposing feeding behaviors following activation
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Mushroom body circuits play a role in processing naïve taste responses.
source: Together, these results establish the STROBE as a new tool for dissecting fly feeding circuits and suggest a role for mushroom body circuits in processing naïve taste responses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster has emerged as a leading model for understanding sensory processing related to food approach, avoidance, and consumption behaviors.
source: Drosophila melanogaster has emerged as a leading model for understanding sensory processing related to food approach, avoidance, and consumption behaviors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Much remains to be learned about the neural circuits that process taste information in the fly brain.
source: However, although the gustatory system is recognized as mediating a critical final checkpoint in determining food suitability, much remains to be learned about the neural circuits that process taste information in the fly brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Flies detect several taste modalities, each of which promotes food acceptance or rejection, similar to mammals.
source: Like mammals, flies detect several taste modalities, each of which promotes food acceptance or rejection (Liman et al., 2014; Marella et al., 2006; Yarmolinsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Taste compounds activate gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) localized on the fly's proboscis, legs, wings, and ovipositor.
source: Taste compounds activate gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) localized on the fly's proboscis, legs, wings, and ovipositor (Scott, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cells expressing the Gustatory Receptor Gr64f respond to sweet compounds and induce strong acceptance behavior.
source: Among the different classes of GRNs present, cells expressing the Gustatory Receptor Gr64f respond to sweet compounds and induce strong acceptance behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: GRNs labeled by Gr66a respond to bitter compounds and evoke avoidance.
source: Conversely, GRNs labeled by Gr66a respond to bitter compounds and evoke avoidance (Dahanukar et al., 2001; Dahanukar et al., 2007; Jiao et al., 2008; Kwon et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2011; Marella et al., 2006; Thorne et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: GRNs connect directly or indirectly to the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the fly brain.
source: GRNs connect directly or indirectly to the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the fly brain (Ito et al., 2014; Rajashekhar and Singh, 1994; Scott, 2018; Stocker and Schorderet, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Taste processing in the SEZ involves local modulatory interneurons.
source: Taste processing in the SEZ involves local modulatory interneurons (Chu et al., 2014; Pool et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Taste processing in the SEZ involves second-order neurons projecting locally or to other brain regions.
source: second-order neurons projecting locally or to other brain regions (Kain and Dahanukar, 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Yapici et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Taste processing in the SEZ involves motor neurons driving feeding subprograms.
source: motor neurons driving feeding subprograms (Gordon and Scott, 2009; Hampel et al., 2011; Manzo et al., 2012; Rajashekhar and Singh, 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Taste processing in the SEZ involves command neurons driving the complete feeding program.
source: and command neurons driving the complete feeding program (Flood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Taste processing is involved in acute feeding events.
source: Taste processing is not only involved in acute feeding events, but also in the formation of associative memories
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Taste processing is involved in the formation of associative memories.
source: Taste processing is not only involved in acute feeding events, but also in the formation of associative memories
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Associative memories are aversive following exposure to bitter taste.
source: which are aversive following exposure to bitter taste (Masek et al., 2015; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Associative memories are positive following sugar consumption.
source: or positive following sugar consumption (Tempel et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Memory formation occurs mainly in a central brain structure called the mushroom body (MB).
source: Memory formation occurs mainly in a central brain structure called the mushroom body (MB), composed of ~2000 Kenyon cells per hemisphere (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The mushroom body is composed of approximately 2000 Kenyon cells per hemisphere.
source: Memory formation occurs mainly in a central brain structure called the mushroom body (MB), composed of ~2000 Kenyon cells per hemisphere (Heisenberg et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The MBs receive sensory information that is assigned a positive or negative output valence via coincident input from dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
source: The MBs receive sensory information that is assigned a positive or negative output valence via coincident input from dopaminergic neurons (DANs) (Perisse et al., 2013; Waddell, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Little is known about how taste information is relayed to the MBs.
source: Little is known about how taste information is relayed to the MBs
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Taste projection neurons (TPNs) connected to bitter GRNs indirectly drive activation of the paired posterior lateral cluster 1 (PPL1) DANs.
source: but taste projection neurons (TPNs) connected to bitter GRNs indirectly drive activation of the paired posterior lateral cluster 1 (PPL1) DANs (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: PPL1 neurons signal punishment to MBs.
source: PPL1 neurons signal punishment to MBs and are required for aversive taste memory formation (Aso et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2010; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2017; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Masek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PPL1 neurons are required for aversive taste memory formation.
source: PPL1 neurons signal punishment to MBs and are required for aversive taste memory formation (Aso et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2010; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2017; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Masek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The protocerebrum anterior medial (PAM) cluster of DANs signals rewarding information.
source: Conversely, the protocerebrum anterior medial (PAM) cluster of DANs signals rewarding information and is involved in the formation of appetitive memories (Burke et al., 2012; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The PAM cluster of DANs is involved in the formation of appetitive memories.
source: Conversely, the protocerebrum anterior medial (PAM) cluster of DANs signals rewarding information and is involved in the formation of appetitive memories (Burke et al., 2012; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PPL1 and PAM involvement in feeding has not been extensively investigated.
source: Although they have well-established roles in memory formation, PPL1 and PAM involvement in feeding has not been extensively investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Kenyon cells and DANs make connections to specific mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) within discrete compartments of the MBs.
source: Kenyon cells and DANs make connections to specific mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) within discrete compartments of the MBs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: MBONs project to protocerebral integration centers.
source: MBONs project to protocerebral integration centers and are required for memory formation and retrieval (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Aso et al., 2014b; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Ichinose et al., 2015; Masek et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Plaçais et al., 2013; Séjourné et al., 2011; Takemura et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MBONs are required for memory formation and retrieval.
source: MBONs project to protocerebral integration centers and are required for memory formation and retrieval (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Aso et al., 2014b; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Ichinose et al., 2015; Masek et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Plaçais et al., 2013; Séjourné et al., 2011; Takemura et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DAN/MBON pairs innervating a specific MB compartment produce behavioral responses of opposing valence.
source: An emerging model is that DAN/MBON pairs innervating a specific MB compartment produce behavioral responses of opposing valence, and that KC-MBON synapses in that compartment are depressed upon DAN activation (Cohn et al., 2015; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents an emerging model in the field.

claim: KC-MBON synapses in a specific MB compartment are depressed upon DAN activation.
source: An emerging model is that DAN/MBON pairs innervating a specific MB compartment produce behavioral responses of opposing valence, and that KC-MBON synapses in that compartment are depressed upon DAN activation (Cohn et al., 2015; Felsenberg et al., 2017; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents an emerging model in the field.

claim: MBONs modulate innate behaviors such as taste sensitivity.
source: While MBONs are known to modulate innate behaviors such as taste sensitivity (Masek et al., 2015) and food seeking behavior (Tsao et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MBONs modulate food seeking behavior.
source: While MBONs are known to modulate innate behaviors such as taste sensitivity (Masek et al., 2015) and food seeking behavior (Tsao et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The possible contribution of MB input and output circuits to feeding behavior remains unclear.
source: the possible contribution of MB input and output circuits to feeding behavior remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Silencing neuron populations in freely behaving flies is a straightforward way to determine their necessity in feeding.
source: Silencing neuron populations in freely behaving flies, which forces the neurons into a chronic 'off' state to mimic a situation where the fly never encounters an activating stimulus, is a straightforward way to determine their necessity in feeding. (Fischler et al., 2007; Gordon and Scott, 2009; LeDue et al., 2015; LeDue et al., 2016; Mann et al., 2013; Marella et al., 2012; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gain-of-function experiments for feeding and taste are more complicated than silencing experiments.
source: However, gain-of-function experiments for feeding and taste, or any other actively sensed stimulus, are more complicated.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental methodology and its challenges.

claim: Behaviors produced by forcing a neuron into a stimulus- and behavior-independent 'on' state can be difficult to interpret.
source: Behaviors produced by forcing a neuron into a stimulus- and behavior-independent 'on' state can be difficult to interpret.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental methodology and its challenges.

claim: Three new systems for closed-loop optogenetic control of feeding flies have emerged: the optoPAD, STROBE, and optoFLIC.
source: Recently, three new systems for closed-loop optogenetic control of feeding flies have emerged: the optoPAD and STROBE, developed as additions to the FlyPAD system; and the optoFLIC, built on the FLIC platform (Jaeger et al., 2018; May et al., 2019; Moreira et al., 2019; Ro et al., 2014; Steck et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The FlyPAD produces capacitance signals that reflect a fly's interaction with food in either of two sensors in a small arena.
source: The FlyPAD produces capacitance signals that reflect a fly's interaction with food in either of two sensors (or 'channels') in a small arena (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Itskov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and reference to figures.

claim: When a fly physically bridges the two electrodes of a sensor by standing on one electrode and making contact with food sitting on the other, it produces a rise in capacitance.
source: When a fly physically bridges the two electrodes of a sensor by standing on one electrode and making contact with food sitting on the other, it produces a rise in capacitance.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the FlyPAD system.

claim: The FlyPAD capacitance signal is acquired at 100 Hz.
source: This signal, which is acquired at 100 Hz, is then decoded post hoc by an algorithm designed to identify sipping events.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the FlyPAD system.

claim: The STROBE tracks the raw capacitance signal in real-time and triggers lighting within the arena during sips.
source: We designed the STROBE to track the raw capacitance signal in real-time and trigger lighting within the arena during sips (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the design and function of the STROBE system.

claim: The latency of LED activation following a touch was 37 ± 17 ms.
source: Based on video captured at 178 frames per second, the latency of LED activation following a touch was 37 ± 17 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measured value from experimental data.

claim: The latency of LED activation is short enough to ensure LED triggering during sips, which generally last longer than 100 ms.
source: This latency is short enough to ensure LED triggering during sips, which generally last longer than 100 ms (Itskov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on measured latency and cited sip duration.

claim: Video of flies feeding in the STROBE consistently showed light activation in the same frame as the fly's proboscis fully extending onto the food.
source: Indeed, video of flies feeding in the STROBE, shot at 60 frames per second, consistently showed light activation in the same frame as the fly's proboscis fully extending onto the food (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from video data.

claim: There is a strong correlation (R2 = 0.963) between the number of sips detected by the FlyPAD algorithm and the number of LED illuminations triggered by the STROBE algorithm.
source: Here, there is a strong correlation between the two (R2 = 0.963), with the number of LED illuminations triggered by the STROBE algorithm being about 1.4 times the number of sips detected by the FlyPAD algorithm.
evidence: This is a statistical measure from experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The number of LED illuminations triggered by the STROBE algorithm is about 1.4 times the number of sips detected by the FlyPAD algorithm.
source: Here, there is a strong correlation between the two (R2 = 0.963), with the number of LED illuminations triggered by the STROBE algorithm being about 1.4 times the number of sips detected by the FlyPAD algorithm.
evidence: This is a measured ratio from experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The increased number of LED activations compared to FlyPAD-detected sips is likely the consequence of the FlyPAD algorithm filtering out capacitance changes not adhering to certain criteria of shape and duration.
source: This increased number is likely the consequence of the FlyPAD algorithm filtering out capacitance changes not adhering to certain criteria of shape and duration (Itskov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of the FlyPAD algorithm and cited prior work.

claim: A fraction of LED activations in the STROBE are triggered by more fleeting interactions with the food rather than full sips.
source: Thus, we expect that a fraction of LED activations in the STROBE are actually triggered by more fleeting interactions with the food. Indeed, video of flies in the STROBE confirmed that a subset of leg touches triggered light activation (Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference confirmed by video observation.

claim: Flies expressing functional CsChrimson in sweet neurons under the control of Gr64f-GAL4 showed a dramatic preference towards feeding on the light-triggering food.
source: Under these conditions, flies expressing functional CsChrimson in sweet neurons under the control of Gr64f-GAL4 showed a dramatic preference towards feeding on the light-triggering food, while control flies of the same genotype that were not pre-fed all-trans-retinal, and thus carried non-functional CsChrimson, displayed no preference (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2.

claim: Control flies not pre-fed all-trans-retinal displayed no preference for the light-triggering food.
source: Under these conditions, flies expressing functional CsChrimson in sweet neurons under the control of Gr64f-GAL4 showed a dramatic preference towards feeding on the light-triggering food, while control flies of the same genotype that were not pre-fed all-trans-retinal, and thus carried non-functional CsChrimson, displayed no preference (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2.

claim: The number of interactions on the light-triggering side of the chamber was dependent on light intensity for Gr64f-GAL4 flies, with increasing interactions up to 6.5 mW/cm2.
source: The number of interactions on the light-triggering side of the chamber was dependent on light intensity, with increasing interactions up 6.5 mW/cm2, above which interaction numbers decreased as a function of intensity.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For Gr64f-GAL4 flies, interaction numbers decreased above 6.5 mW/cm2 light intensity.
source: The number of interactions on the light-triggering side of the chamber was dependent on light intensity, with increasing interactions up 6.5 mW/cm2, above which interaction numbers decreased as a function of intensity.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Preference for the light-triggering food was relatively stable above a threshold of 1.85 mW/cm2 for Gr64f-GAL4 flies.
source: However, preference was relatively stable above a threshold of 1.85 mW/cm2 (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Interactions generally accumulated linearly over time at all intensities for Gr64f-GAL4 flies.
source: Additionally, interactions generally accumulated linearly over time at all intensities, with a stable preference index established within the first 15 min of a one-hour experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A stable preference index was established within the first 15 min of a one-hour experiment for Gr64f-GAL4 flies.
source: Additionally, interactions generally accumulated linearly over time at all intensities, with a stable preference index established within the first 15 min of a one-hour experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither sensitization nor adaptation occurs during the course of the experiment for Gr64f-GAL4 flies.
source: This suggests that neither sensitization nor adaptation occurs during the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear accumulation of interactions over time.

claim: The flies do not appear to adjust their behavior in response to the perceived mismatch between the sweet taste and lack of energy content of the food source.
source: Moreover, the flies do not appear to adjust their behavior in response to the perceived mismatch between the sweet taste and lack of energy content of the food source.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stable preference over time.

claim: Flies expressing functional CsChrimson in bitter sensing neurons under the control of Gr66a-GAL4 strongly avoided neuronal activation in the STROBE by engaging in fewer interactions with the light-triggering food source.
source: As expected, flies expressing functional CsChrimson in bitter sensing neurons under the control of Gr66a-GAL4 strongly avoided neuronal activation in the STROBE by engaging in fewer interactions with the light-triggering food source (Figure 2F–J).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2F-J.

claim: The behavioral response of Gr66a-GAL4 flies was intensity-dependent, with maximum suppression of interactions occurring at the highest intensity tested (16.4 mW/cm2).
source: Once again the behavioral response was intensity-dependent, with maximum suppression of interactions occurring at the highest intensity tested (16.4 mW/cm2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2J.

claim: For Gr66a-GAL4 flies, preference develops in roughly the first 15 min and remains relatively stable for the rest of the hour.
source: As with sweet GRN activation, the flies' preference develops in roughly the first 15 min and remains relatively stable for the rest of the hour (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The changes in food interactions driven by GRN activation are accompanied by strong effects on food ingestion in the expected direction.
source: In all cases, these studies confirmed that the changes in food interactions driven by GRN activation are accompanied by strong effects on food ingestion in the expected direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 using dye ingestion assays.

claim: Starvation duration has a well-known impact on fly feeding – the longer flies are food deprived, the more they will initiate and sustain feeding on sweet foods.
source: Starvation duration has a well-known impact on fly feeding – the longer flies are food deprived, the more they will initiate and sustain feeding on sweet foods (Dus et al., 2013; Dus et al., 2011; Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; Scheiner et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Starvation increased flies' preference for the light-triggering food in the STROBE when their sweet neurons expressed functional CsChrimson.
source: Consistent with its effect on sugar feeding, starvation increased flies' preference for the light-triggering food in the STROBE when their sweet neurons expressed functional CsChrimson (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The elevated preference index driven by starvation is driven by a dramatic increase in interaction number for Gr64f-GAL4 flies.
source: This elevated preference index is driven by a dramatic increase in interaction number (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Starvation had no significant effect on light avoidance mediated by bitter neuron activation under the tested conditions.
source: In contrast to its impact on sweet sensory neurons, starvation had no significant effect on light avoidance mediated by bitter neuron activation under these conditions (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Starvation had little to no effect on the timing of food choice throughout the assay for both Gr64f-GAL4 and Gr66a-GAL4 flies.
source: Starvation also had little to no effect on the timing of food choice throughout the assay, with all groups establishing their peak preference within the first 10–15 min and largely maintaining it throughout the assay (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Adding increasing concentrations of sucrose to both food options caused dose-dependent inhibition of Gr64f > CsChrimson flies' preference for the light-triggering food.
source: Indeed, adding increasing concentrations of sucrose to both food options caused dose-dependent inhibition of GR64f > CsChrimson flies' preference for the light-triggering food (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The change in preference driven by sucrose addition is driven by a progressively higher number of interactions on the no-light side, with relatively constant interaction numbers on the light side as sucrose concentration increases for Gr64f > CsChrimson flies.
source: This change is driven by a progressively higher number of interactions on the no-light side, with relatively constant interaction numbers on the light side as sucrose concentration increases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The addition of sucrose mildly enhanced the negative preferences driven by STROBE activation of Gr66a bitter neurons.
source: On the other hand, the addition of sucrose mildly enhanced the negative preferences driven by STROBE activation of Gr66a bitter neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The addition of denatonium to both sides caused dose-dependent inhibition of the aversion shown by Gr66a > CsChrimson flies.
source: The same pattern is mirrored by the addition of the bitter compound denatonium to both sides: dose-dependent inhibition of the aversion shown by Gr66a > CsChrimson flies (Figure 4D,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The addition of denatonium had little to no effect on the attraction of Gr64f > CsChrimson flies to the light side.
source: and little to no effect on the attraction of Gr64f > CsChrimson flies to the light side (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: No substantial change in preference was observed after establishment in the first 10–15 min for experiments with chemical taste ligands.
source: In general, as with other experiments, we observed no substantial change in preference after establishment in the first 10–15 min (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2–5.

claim: Flies are not displaying satiety effects from sugar ingestion or taste-independent effects from the consumption of denatonium.
source: This suggests that flies are not displaying satiety effects from sugar ingestion or taste-independent effects from the consumption of denatonium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stable preference over time.

claim: Fdg activation in the STROBE produced an extremely high number of interactions on the light-triggering food, resulting in a nearly complete preference for that side.
source: Strikingly, Fdg activation in the STROBE produced an extremely high number of interactions on the light-triggering food, resulting in a nearly complete preference for that side (Figure 5; Video 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5 and Video 2.

claim: The STROBE can effectively modulate feeding behavior via the activation of either peripheral or central neurons.
source: Thus, the STROBE can effectively modulate feeding behavior via the activation of either peripheral or central neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results with both GRNs and Fdg neurons.

claim: Flies expressing functional CsChrimson in the α3/α'3 subset of PPL1 dopaminergic neurons (MB308B-GAL4) showed a negative preference towards light when 100 mM sucrose was present in both options.
source: Flies expressing functional CsChrimson in the α3/α'3 subset of PPL1 dopaminergic neurons (MB308B-GAL4) showed a negative preference towards light when 100 mM sucrose was present in both options, but not if the food was plain agar (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Flies expressing functional CsChrimson in the α3/α'3 subset of PPL1 dopaminergic neurons (MB308B-GAL4) did not show a negative preference towards light if the food was plain agar.
source: Flies expressing functional CsChrimson in the α3/α'3 subset of PPL1 dopaminergic neurons (MB308B-GAL4) showed a negative preference towards light when 100 mM sucrose was present in both options, but not if the food was plain agar (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Activation of a broader subset of PPL1 neurons (MB065B-GAL4) led to stronger avoidance in the presence of 100 mM sucrose or plain agar.
source: Performing the same experiment with activation of a broader subset of PPL1 neurons (MB065B-GAL4) led to stronger avoidance in the presence of 100 mM sucrose or plain agar (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Activation of MBONs post-synaptic to PPL1 (MB093C-GAL4 and MB026B-GAL4) produced strong attraction in either context (agar or sucrose).
source: Interestingly, activation of MBONs post-synaptic to PPL1 (MB093C-GAL4 and MB026B-GAL4) produced strong attraction in either context (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Activating the β2m,β'2p PAM subset (MB056B-GAL4 and MB301B-GAL4) in the STROBE led to attraction.
source: Indeed, activating the β2m,β'2 p PAM subset (MB056B-GAL4 and MB301B-GAL4) in the STROBE led to attraction (Figure 6F,G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6F,G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activating the corresponding β2m,β'2p,γ5 MBONs (MB011B-GAL4 and MB210B-GAL4) produced avoidance when sucrose was present.
source: On the other hand, activating the corresponding β2m,β'2 p,γ5 MBONs (MB011B-GAL4 and MB210B-GAL4) produced avoidance when sucrose was present (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: PAM γ3 neurons were recently shown to encode a negative valence and induce appetitive memories following transient inhibition by the satiety peptide Allatostatin-A.
source: Another subset of PAMs, targeting the γ3 compartment, was recently shown to encode a negative valence and induce appetitive memories following transient inhibition by the satiety peptide Allatostatin-A (Yamagata et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Activation of PAM γ3 neurons (MB441B-GAL4 and MB195B-GAL4) in the STROBE produced light avoidance.
